before: A difficulty forecast can use current difficulty, the block where the next adjustment occurs and the time elapsed between observed Bitcoin blocks. The method needs to identify those blocks and when the inputs were recorded.

Blocks do not arrive at regular intervals. Extending the pace so far into the rest of the adjustment period requires an assumption about future block timing. It does not measure a future network value. The estimated calendar date can change too.
after: Bitcoin adjusts difficulty every 2,016 blocks to target about ten minutes per block. Within its protocol limits, the adjustment scales current difficulty by the target duration divided by the measured duration. Faster blocks point towards a higher next difficulty; slower blocks point towards a lower one.

A simple forecast estimates the full period’s duration by extending the block pace observed so far. It uses that estimate in the adjustment rule to project difficulty. This needs current difficulty, the target block and the observed blocks’ heights and timestamps.

Blocks arrive irregularly, so the pace can change as more arrive. Extending the observed pace assumes it will continue through the remaining blocks. The projected difficulty and calendar date can therefore change; neither is a measured future value.

before: A fair comparison asks each forecast the same question: what will the difficulty change be at the same target block? Use the same definition of difficulty change and compare forecasts issued at the same time. A later forecast has information that an earlier one did not.

Keep each forecast as originally issued, together with its input block height, source, model version and definition of the outcome. Include failed and missing forecasts in the record. Selecting only successful predictions would change the comparison.
after: Compare predictions of the same difficulty change at the same target block, issued at comparable times. A later forecast can use information that an earlier one did not have.

Keep each forecast as originally issued, with its stated range, input block height, source, model version and outcome definition. Record its publication time, including an independently verifiable capture when timing matters. Group forecasts by lead time. Record failed and missing forecasts, as well as the exclusion rules; selecting only successful predictions would change the comparison.
note: Combines the complete comparison-record requirements here, including range, input height, target/time, source, version, outcome, independent capture, missing/failed forecasts and exclusions. These no longer need a second inventory in the observed report (habits 3, 6, 7).

before: Error and forecast ranges
after: Point errors and ranges answer different questions
note: Explains what each result teaches instead of repeating a parallel checklist. Preserves sample-only meaning, width/inclusion trade-off and independent-observation requirements for testing confidence (habits 3, 6).

before: Absolute error is the size of the gap between a forecast and its outcome. Mean absolute error averages those gaps across the forecasts being tested. It describes that sample, not how the model will perform in another period.

A forecast range needs a separate test. How often did it contain the outcome, and how wide was it? A wide range can contain many outcomes while telling you little. Testing whether ranges match their stated confidence level needs enough independent observations over a clearly defined period.
after: Absolute error is the size of the gap between a forecast and its outcome. Mean absolute error averages those gaps across the forecasts tested. A smaller mean means the point estimates were closer on average in that sample; it does not establish performance in another period.

Ranges answer a different question: how often did they contain the outcome? Read that share alongside their width, since a wide range can contain many outcomes while telling you little. Testing a stated confidence level needs enough independent observations over a defined period.
note: Explains what each result teaches instead of repeating a parallel checklist. Preserves sample-only meaning, width/inclusion trade-off and independent-observation requirements for testing confidence (habits 3, 6).

before: The source is the mempool.space one-year difficulty-adjustment API, captured on 22 October 2026. To repeat the calculation, sort its 26 adjustment blocks by height and check that consecutive blocks are 2,016 blocks apart. Exclude the earliest: its preceding difficulty is outside the snapshot. For each remaining adjustment, calculate 100 × (new difficulty / previous difficulty − 1). Do not use the provider’s rounded adjustment ratio.

The mean absolute change averages the size of the 25 percentage changes, ignoring whether each is positive or negative. Calculations retain the provider’s full difficulty precision; rounding affects only the display. The citation manifest lists SHA-256 digests, which are file checksums, for the original response and CSV/JSON downloads. These let readers detect changes from this version.
